frameworks.name: Topical Authority
frameworks.definition: Topical Authority is a positive ranking state that a website achieves when it demonstrates deep, comprehensive, and semantically connected coverage of a topic. It is founded on the concept that search engines evaluate a source's expertise and trustworthiness based on its topical map, historical data, and ability to satisfy user intent across related queries. Koray defines it as a measure of how well a web entity covers a knowledge domain with contextual relevance and consistency, leading to higher initial rankings and re-ranking advantages.
methods: 1. Create a topical map by identifying the main topic, entities, attributes, and their relationships.
2. Expand the topical map by covering more entities of the same type, covering more attributes of existing entities, and deepening context with further consistency.
3. Use contextual bridges to connect different topical areas (e.g., from energy to credit via 'money saving' context).
4. Define and optimize Source Context (primary focus of the website) and Brand Identity.
5. Implement query-focused semantic vocabulary configuration: align the vocabulary of queries and documents, canonicalize verbs and nouns based on query patterns.
6. Use predicates (verbs) to create semantically connected content networks; leverage Frame Semantics and Semantic Role Labels.
7. Ensure symmetry and consistency across multilingual versions (if applicable) to share PageRank and quality signals via hreflang.
8. Prioritize tasks for international SEO using principles of Prioritization, Symmetry, Matchability, and Consistency.
9. Apply Technical SEO to reduce cost of retrieval (crawl efficiency, page speed, clean indexation).
10. Use Local SEO and brand SERP optimization to build trust and real-world identity.
11. Train authors to maintain discipline and consistency in semantic content creation.
12. Continuously monitor and adjust based on search engine tolerance, source prioritization, and comparative ranking.
frameworks.unique_position: Koray's Topical Authority framework differs from generic SEO advice by being deeply grounded in semantics, search engine patents, and rigorous case studies with open data. It emphasizes a holistic, philosophical approach that requires understanding how search engines think, not just following checklists. Key differentiators include: (1) focus on 'predicates' and 'verbs of life' to model user behavior, (2) use of Frame Semantics and Semantic Role Labels, (3) insistence on discipline and consistency to avoid topical map distortion, (4) integration of multilingual and cross-lingual principles, (5) emphasis on 'Source Context' and 'Brand Identity' as foundational, and (6) reliance on real-world performance metrics (naked Google Search Console data) rather than tool-based estimates. Koray positions his work as a 'change in SEO culture' rather than a set of tactics.
frameworks.evolution: Koray Gubur conceptualized and defined Topical Authority in the 'Importance of Topical Authority Case Study' and has since expanded it through multiple case studies and publications. The framework has evolved from initial concepts (Topical Borders, Topical Maps) to include deeper semantic layers (Source Context, Brand Identity, Contextual Bridges) and advanced topics like Cross-lingual Information Retrieval and Comparative Ranking. It has become a mainstream SEO concept, but Koray emphasizes that his version is rooted in search engine patents, real-world data, and a philosophical understanding of semantics. The latest research includes 26 full-scale SEO studies and the upcoming Semantic SEO Course.
frameworks.evidence: Koray cites multiple real-world SEO case studies with specific performance metrics, including: Teamcolorcodes.com (110% organic click increase, 7,000+ top 1-3 ranking queries), Kanbanize.com (245% organic click increase, 39,000 new ranking queries), Snuffstore.de (1200% organic click increase), Encazip.com (from 10,000 to 500,000+ organic clicks), TheCoolist.com (120% organic click increase, 561,000+ total ranking queries), Complaintsboard.com (320% organic click increase), BKMKitap.com (350% organic click increase, became 6th largest e-commerce in Turkey), Diyetkolik.com (200% organic click increase), and a project reaching 1,000,000 organic clicks from zero. He also references Google patents (e.g., 'Candidate Answer Passage Scoring', 'Information Extraction from Database', 'Systems and methods for generating extraction models', 'Modifying search result ranking based on implicit user feedback', 'Language classifiers for language detection') and research by Sergey Brin, Justin Boyan, and Charles Fillmore. The framework is supported by open Google Search Console data and client testimonials.
frameworks.nuances: Koray emphasizes several subtle points and warnings: (1) Topical Authority is a 'positive ranking state' that can be lost if the topical map is distorted (e.g., by adding low-quality pages for small queries). (2) 'Comparative Ranking' means that quality thresholds change over time; a top-quality article today may become mediocre as competitors improve. (3) 'Search Engine Tolerance' and 'Source Prioritization' mean that once a source proves itself, it can retain rankings even if technical SEO improvements are lost. (4) 'Cost of Retrieval' must be balanced: high-quality content justifies higher crawl costs, but bloated sites with unnecessary pages harm authority. (5) 'Entity stuffing' is as bad as keyword stuffing; each sentence should provide a new fact. (6) Training authors is the biggest obstacle; semantic content networks require a disciplined, structured mindset. (7) For multilingual sites, symmetry and consistency across languages are critical; asymmetry can cause demotion. (8) 'Inorganic site structure' (different designs/topics across language versions) can trigger spam detection. (9) The framework is not a one-time effort; continuous improvement and 'Comparative Ranking' require ongoing optimization. (10) Koray warns that his methods are hard to replicate without deep understanding of semantics and philosophy; he recommends lawyers, sociologists, and psychology readers as naturally better suited for semantic SEO.

frameworks.name: Semantic SEO
frameworks.definition: Semantic SEO is the practice of optimizing a website or web page for semantic search engines to improve its ranking and visibility, developed in the 2010s as a response to the increasing use of semantic search technology. It requires understanding search engines and the philosophy of knowledge, focusing on meaning, context, and entity relationships rather than keywords. Koray frames it as a discipline that leverages semantic content networks, topical authority, and the 'verbs of life' to align with how search engines understand human language and behavior.
methods: 1. Identify the Source Context (brand purpose, target audience) to sharpen and deepen the context.
2. Select canonical verbs (predicates) and nouns that represent core behaviors and outcomes (e.g., 'learn', 'earn', 'improve').
3. Create Semantic Content Networks by connecting verb-noun pairs across related contexts (e.g., 'Universities and Occupations', 'Occupations and Salaries').
4. Use FrameNet and Semantic Role Labels to structure content around frames (e.g., for 'cook': heat source, tool, recipe).
5. Perform Query-Focused Semantic Vocabulary Configuration: align document vocabulary with query patterns, using synonyms and phrase taxonomies.
6. Sculpt the context by refining verb and noun connections to a specific domain (e.g., restaurants vs. students).
7. Expand topical maps by finding topical gaps and using contextual bridges (e.g., from 'energy' to 'credit' via 'money saving').
8. Implement entity-oriented search: ensure the brand is recognized as a real-world entity (string vs. thing) via Knowledge Graph and consistent signals.
9. Maintain military discipline: avoid distorting the topical map for small queries, complete all semantic content networks, and ensure author training.
frameworks.unique_position: Koray's Semantic SEO differs from generic SEO by centering on 'verbs of life' (predicates) as the foundation for understanding search behavior and creating content networks. He emphasizes military discipline, consistency, and completing all semantic content networks to avoid being labeled a half-authority. His approach integrates philosophy of knowledge, real-world case studies with naked data, and practical use of FrameNet and semantic role labels. He distinguishes between 'strings' and 'things' (entities) and insists on training authors and maintaining momentum to protect topical authority.
frameworks.evolution: Koray conceptualized and defined Topical Authority as a core part of Semantic SEO, first introduced in the 'Importance of Topical Authority Case Study'. The framework has evolved from initial keyword-based approaches to a structured methodology involving semantic content networks, predicates, and FrameNet. He has published multiple case studies (e.g., TheCoolist, Encazip, Sunnyvalley.io) that demonstrate iterative refinement, with updates showing increased organic traffic and ranking queries. The upcoming Semantic SEO Course aims to formalize the training, moving from macro-semantics to micro-semantics optimization.

frameworks.name: Holistic SEO
frameworks.definition: Holistic SEO is the process of developing integrated digital marketing projects with every aspect including coding, Natural Language Processing, Data Science, Page Speed, Digital Analytics, Content Marketing, Technical SEO, and Branding. It focuses on improving a brand's organic visibility and growth potential through entity-based Search Engine Optimization, recognizing that structured, semantic search engines now detect real-world entities and that a simple website is no longer sufficient to demonstrate authority, trustworthiness, and expertise.
methods: Expand topical maps by covering more entities, attributes, and deepening context using taxonomies and ontologies.
Create contextual bridges between different topics to connect semantic content networks.
Use content item brief templates and content item article templates for scalable content creation.
Perform SEO A/B tests to understand search engine algorithms and decision trees.
Apply NLP and automation for large-scale sites (e.g., using Python for word clouds, data analysis).
Train authors to follow semantic SEO principles and maintain disciplined thinking.
Analyze log files to optimize crawl efficiency and understand search engine behavior.
Implement technical SEO improvements (crawl budget, canonicalization, page speed, JavaScript SEO, etc.).
Use data science algorithms (e.g., clustering queries, understanding word proximity) to inform content strategy.
Conduct local SEO optimization (Google My Business, Apple Maps, Yandex, Yellow Pages).
Perform conversion rate optimization for e-commerce and event-based websites.
frameworks.unique_position: Koray's Holistic SEO differs from generic SEO by integrating multiple disciplines (coding, NLP, data science, branding, etc.) into a single framework, emphasizing entity-based optimization and topical authority over keyword-focused tactics. It is grounded in deep analysis of search engine patents and algorithms, with a strong theoretical foundation derived from Bill Slawski's work. The approach is validated through extensive case studies with multiple websites and open data, aiming to change SEO culture by promoting a disciplined, structured mindset. Koray positions his methodology as more academic and rigorous, requiring continuous learning and adaptation, and he explicitly criticizes superficial SEO practices that lack testing and data science understanding.
frameworks.evolution: Holistic SEO was founded on 1 September 2020 by Koray Tuğberk GÜBÜR as a one-man company, later growing to over 6 employees. The framework has evolved through continuous publication of case studies and research, introducing concepts such as Topical Authority, Source Context, Brand Identity, and Contextual Bridges. It draws heavily from Bill Slawski's patent analysis and search philosophy, which Koray credits as the origin of the Topical Authority concept. The framework has been refined over time with new sub-concepts and practical methodologies, and Koray plans to launch a Semantic SEO Course to further disseminate the approach.

frameworks.name: Entity-Based SEO
frameworks.definition: Entity-Based SEO is a framework that shifts focus from keywords (strings) to real-world entities (things). It involves optimizing a brand or entity to be recognized, understood, and trusted by search engines and AI systems as a distinct, authoritative entity within Google's Knowledge Graph. The goal is to transform a brand from a mere string into a recognized entity with a stable Knowledge Panel, thereby improving its prominence, credibility, and relevance in search results and AI assistive engines.
core_concepts: N.E.E.A.T.T (Notability, Experience, Expertise, Authoritativeness, Trustworthiness, Transparency)
methods: 1. Create an Entity Group in Kalicube Pro with entity name, type, and entity home.
2. Define Entity Subtitle and Entity Qualifier Word to disambiguate the entity.
3. Provide primary domain and audience information.
4. Add Knowledge Graph ID (kgmid), Wikipedia Article, and Wikidata URL if available.
5. Set locations (up to 5) to track Knowledge Panel variations by language and region.
6. Use Kalicube Pro's Knowledge Graph Explorer to identify duplicate entities and perform entity reconciliation.
7. In the Knowledge Panel tasks section, follow a 6-step process: Entity Home, Description, Fundamental Facts, Classify, Schema, Corroboration.
8. Write a description with subtitle, short description, and description extension; use NLP analysis via Google's NLP API.
9. Add fundamental facts (basic factual information).
10. Classify knowledge resources (web pages) that affect the entity's Knowledge Graph presence using filters (profile, review, data source, etc.).
11. Generate Schema.org markup based on provided information and add it to the entity home.
12. Add corroboration pages to confirm entity information from third-party sources.
13. Monitor Knowledge Graph Score and Brand SERP Control over time.
14. Use NLP Entity Analysis on Brand SERP to understand how Google perceives the entity.
15. Expand topical maps by covering more entities, attributes, and deepening context with contextual bridges.
16. Use Python and Google Knowledge Graph API (via Advertools) to analyze entity profiles, relevance scores, and entity relations.
frameworks.unique_position: Koray Gubur's Entity-Based SEO is distinct from generic SEO advice by focusing on the technical and semantic aspects of entity identity and reconciliation. It emphasizes making a brand a recognized entity in Google's Knowledge Graph through precise control of entity homes, descriptions, and corroboration from authoritative sources. Unlike traditional SEO that targets keywords, this framework uses tools like Kalicube Pro for detailed Knowledge Panel management and Python for data-driven analysis of entity relations. Koray notes that RankBrain marks a shift from keyword-centric SEO to semantic structure and entity importance. His own framework integrates these historical developments into a holistic SEO approach that leverages historical data, broad appeal, and cross-language information retrieval.

frameworks.name: Content Quality & Linguistics
frameworks.definition: Koray Gubur defines content quality as the degree to which digital content provides unique, relevant, and valuable information that satisfies user search intent, while linguistics refers to the precise and correct use of language—including spelling, grammar, and word choice—to maintain Expertise, Authoritativeness, and Trustworthiness (E-A-T). He emphasizes that thin content is not merely short text but any content that fails to deliver added value, even if lengthy, and that linguistic accuracy directly impacts SEO and user experience.
methods: Improve dwell time by: 1) Simple design, 2) Conduct user research, 3) Personalize content, 4) Optimize website structure, 5) Improve content quality, 6) Optimize load time, 7) Use calls-to-action, 8) Use gamification, 9) Use internal linking, 10) Use visuals and multimedia.

Fix thin content by: 1) Delete the page, 2) Set to noindex, 3) Fill with unique content, 4) Combine multiple thin pages into one comprehensive piece, 5) Update outdated content, 6) Use bullets and concise formatting.

Fix linguistic errors by: 1) Spell check and proofread manually, 2) Ask a colleague to review, 3) Read content aloud, 4) Use online tools (e.g., Copyscape, Google Analytics, SEMrush), 5) Understand etymology and spelling rules (e.g., double consonants, suffix addition).
frameworks.unique_position: Koray's approach differs from generic SEO advice by treating content quality and linguistics as inseparable components of a holistic strategy. He argues that even long, detailed content can be considered 'thin' if it does not provide unique value or satisfy user intent, and that linguistic precision (correct spelling, grammar, word choice) directly influences E-A-T and search rankings. He uses data science and A/B testing to empirically understand search engine algorithms, and emphasizes that content must be both informative and linguistically flawless to build trust and authority.
frameworks.evolution: The concept of thin content emerged in 2012 after Google's Quality Rater Guidelines were leaked, and the Panda update (2011) penalized low-quality content. Dwell time as a metric gained traction in the late 2000s and became prominent in the 2010s as Google refined algorithms to focus on user experience. Koray's framework integrates these historical developments with a holistic approach, but no explicit versioning of a 'Content Quality & Linguistics' framework is detailed in these documents.

frameworks.name: Multilingual & International SEO
frameworks.definition: Multilingual SEO is the process of optimizing a website or web entity for multiple languages in the context of Search Engine Optimization, closely connected to Multiregional SEO. It aims to acquire visibility across different languages and increase organic traffic for different countries and cultures by leveraging search engines' ability to understand content across languages and benefiting from broad appeal and historical data.

Inorganic Site Structure (avoiding different designs/logos per language)
Canonical Version and Alternate Versions (with hreflang)

methods: 1. Unite multilingual and multiregional SEO using hreflang tags with ISO 639-1 language codes and ISO 3166-1 Alpha 2 region codes.
2. Prioritize SEO tasks by focusing on two key advantages: Broad Appeal and Historical Data, rather than fixing all technical issues.

3. Perform query research for different languages and regions using: Google Keyword Planner with localization filters, SEMRush Keyword Magic Tool, Google Trends, Ahrefs Keyword Planner, Google My Business Performance Report, Amazon/Alibaba keyword tools, and Reddit keyword research tools.
4. Ensure symmetry: every language section should have equivalent content for the same topics, with matching internal link paths and design.
5. Maintain consistency: use the same brand logo, colors, layout, and topic across all language versions to avoid inorganic site structure penalties.
6. For multiple domains: use same logo, cross-referential hreflang, same brand colors, symmetric content, structured data marking same organization, localized GMB accounts, and local servers.
7. For multiple subdomains: internally link each subdomain to the main domain, use hreflang, same brand identity, symmetric content, separate sitemaps/robots.txt/GSC accounts.
8. Prefer subfolders over subdomains or multiple domains for better entity consolidation, PageRank flow, and crawl efficiency.
9. Use International Targeting in Google Search Console only if not using a country-code top-level domain; otherwise let search engines infer targeting from signals.

frameworks.name: Knowledge Graph & Structured Data
frameworks.definition: Koray Gubur defines the Knowledge Graph as a graph of entities and their connections, used by search engines to understand real-world things and move beyond strings to things (Amit Singhal). Structured data (Schema.org) is the mechanism to formally define entities and their attributes, enabling search engines to build and refine the Knowledge Graph. The framework integrates Knowledge Graphs, Knowledge Panels, Brand SERPs, and structured data into a unified entity-based SEO strategy, where the goal is to make a brand a recognized entity with a clear, consistent identity across the web.
core_concepts: N.E.E.A.T.T (Notability, Experience, Expertise, Authoritativeness, Trustworthiness, Transparency)
methods: 1. Create an Entity Group in Kalicube Pro.
2. Add entity with name, type, and entity home (a single page the entity owner controls 100%).
3. Choose Entity Subtitle and Entity Qualifier word to disambiguate.
4. Set primary domain and audience.
5. Add Knowledge Graph ID (kgmid), Wikipedia article, and Wikidata URL.
6. Select locations (up to 5) to track Knowledge Panel variations by language and region.
7. Use Kalicube Pro's Knowledge Graph Explorer to find and reconcile duplicate entities.
8. Perform NLP Entity Analysis on the Brand SERP using Google's NLP API via Kalicube Pro.
9. Classify knowledge resources (profile, review, data source, etc.) and confirm automated classifications.
10. Generate Schema.org markup based on provided entity information and add it to the entity home.
11. Add corroboration pages that confirm the entity description and prominence.
12. Track Knowledge Panel and Brand SERP changes daily, weekly, or monthly.
13. Use the Task Management system to set goals (e.g., remove a negative result, add a SERP feature).
14. For Knowledge Panel management: claim entity, provide consistent info on authoritative sources, give feedback to Google, use Google Knowledge Graph API to audit entity connections.
frameworks.unique_position: Koray's version is entity-first and holistic, integrating Knowledge Graphs, Knowledge Panels, Brand SERPs, and structured data into a single, data-driven workflow. Unlike generic SEO advice that focuses on keywords or backlinks, this framework emphasizes building a coherent entity identity across the open web, using tools like Kalicube Pro to measure Google's confidence in its understanding of the entity (Knowledge Graph Score). It uniquely addresses entity reconciliation (deduping), language/location variations, and the Algorithmic Trinity (search, Knowledge Graphs, LLMs). The approach is grounded in patent analysis and real-world case studies, and it treats Brand SERP as a reflection of Google's opinion of the brand, directly impacting E-E-A-T signals.
frameworks.evolution: The framework has evolved significantly since 2012 when Jason Barnard coined 'Brand SERP'. Kalicube Pro launched in 2015 and has grown to include 9.4 billion brand datapoints covering 70 million brands by 2025. The concept expanded from traditional search to include AI Assistive Engines (ChatGPT, Google AI Mode) and the Algorithmic Trinity. Knowledge Graph algorithm updates (last noted Feb 2022) periodically reshape entity profiles. The framework now incorporates KaliNexus for educating AI systems. Koray's own work on Topical Authority (2022) and the Unibaby case study (transforming a string into an entity) are milestones.

frameworks.name: Python & Data-Driven SEO
frameworks.definition: Python & Data-Driven SEO is the application of Python programming and data science techniques to understand search engines, optimize content, and make data-driven decisions. It involves using Python libraries like NLTK for natural language processing (lemmatization, tokenization, stemming, synonym extraction), log file analysis for crawler behavior, A/B testing for conversion optimization, and data visualization (e.g., word clouds) to derive actionable insights. Koray frames it within Holistic SEO, which is 'the process of developing integrated digital marketing projects with every aspect including coding, Natural Language Processing, Data Science, Page Speed, Digital Analytics, Content Marketing, Technical SEO, and Branding.'
methods: 1. For NLTK Lemmatization: Import WordNetLemmatizer, tokenize text, apply lemmatize() with POS tag (e.g., wordnet.VERB) to get base forms.
2. For NLTK Tokenization: Use word_tokenize() or sent_tokenize(); remove stop words with stopwords.words('english') and punctuation with isalnum(); count tokens with Counter; visualize with pandas.
3. For NLTK Stemming: Import PorterStemmer, tokenize, apply stem() to each token; compare with LancasterStemmer or SnowballStemmer.
4. For Synonym/Antonym Extraction: Use wordnet.synsets() and lemmas() to get synonyms; check antonyms() for opposites; create custom functions with POS filtering.
5. For Log File Analysis: Collect server logs, parse with Python (e.g., pandas), evaluate crawler visits, measure download completions, identify caching issues.
6. For A/B Testing: Form a project team, prioritize hypotheses, run test (classic split or multivariate), evaluate with 95% confidence, document results, implement winning variant.
7. For Word Clouds: Use WordCloud library with mask images; generate from text or DataFrame columns; adjust parameters like max_words, background_color.
frameworks.unique_position: Koray's approach integrates deep technical understanding of search engines (e.g., citing Google patents) with practical Python coding. He emphasizes mimicking search engine processing (using NLTK to understand how search engines lemmatize, tokenize, and extract synonyms) and using data science to test hypotheses (A/B tests, log analysis). It is not generic SEO advice but a systematic, code-driven methodology that treats SEO as an engineering and data science discipline, focusing on entity-based optimization and topical authority.

Conversion & Growth can be understood as the process of attracting, converting, closing, and delighting customers through data-driven, iterative optimization of the user experience across all touchpoints, with the ultimate goal of sustainable business growth.

frameworks.name: SEO Case Study Methodology
frameworks.definition: Koray Gubur defines SEO Case Study Methodology as a rigorous, evidence-based approach to formulating how search engines work and how to convince them through real-world projects. He states, 'an SEO Case Study doesn’t mean SEO Success, it means that you formulate how the search engine works, and how you convinced it.' The methodology involves presenting multiple real-world websites with open, naked data to prove theoretical concepts, rather than using case studies solely for marketing. It is a way to demonstrate the effectiveness of semantic SEO and topical authority principles through documented, repeatable results.
core_concepts: Search Engine Trust and Historical Data
frameworks.methods: Koray provides a multi-step process for creating and expanding semantic content networks, though not as a single numbered list. Key steps include: 1) Identify central predicates (verbs) and nouns from the source context (e.g., 'learn', 'earn', 'improve'). 2) Connect verbs and nouns through natural semantic patterns (e.g., 'learn a skill', 'earn money from that skill'). 3) Sculpt and deepen the context by narrowing the source context to a specific brand purpose (e.g., course selling). 4) Perform query-focused semantic vocabulary configuration to align document vocabulary with query patterns. 5) Use FrameNet and semantic role labels to understand predicate-driven entity connections. 6) Expand topical maps by finding topical gaps and building at least three contextual bridges to related topics. 7) Create content item brief templates and article templates for scalable content engineering. 8) Use entity-oriented search principles to cover all attributes and related entities. 9) Continuously update and refine the semantic content network to maintain comparative ranking advantage. 10) Train authors rigorously to maintain discipline and consistency.
frameworks.unique_position: Koray's version differs from generic SEO advice by using multiple real-world case studies with open, naked data rather than single-website marketing case studies. He focuses on semantics, predicates, and the 'verbs of life' as the foundation for content networks, which is unique. He emphasizes discipline, consistency, and the danger of distorting topical maps for short-term monetization. His methodology combines deep patent analysis with practical implementation, and he insists on proving theories with multiple websites. He also stresses the human side of SEO (training authors, client education) and the need for a 'structured and disciplined mindset'.
frameworks.evolution: The methodology evolved from Koray's study of Bill Slawski's patent analyses and his own early case studies. He published his first SEO Case Study in 2020 (Hangikredi.com). The 'Semantic Content Networks' article was written on 26 May 2022 and later updated with new projects. The 'Topical Authority' concept was formally introduced in the 'Importance of Topical Authority Case Study' and has been refined through multiple case studies (e.g., Encazip updated three times). Koray plans to launch a Semantic SEO Course to further systematize the methodology. Over time, he has emphasized the need for 'military discipline' to prevent topical map distortion and has added concepts like 'Comparative Ranking' and 'Cost of Retrieval'.
frameworks.evidence: Koray cites Bill Slawski extensively as the primary source of inspiration and theoretical foundation. He references Google patents (e.g., 'Candidate Answer Passage Scoring', 'Efficient index for low latency search of large graphs', 'Information Extraction from Database'), Sergey Brin's research, FrameNet, and NLTK. He provides screenshots from Google Search Console, Ahrefs, and SEMrush as evidence of organic growth. He includes client testimonials from Paul Jensen, Dimitar Karaivanov, Alex Ion, and others. He also mentions his own A/B tests and the use of multiple websites to prove each concept.
frameworks.nuances: Koray emphasizes 'military discipline' – once a topical map is created, it must not be distorted by adding pages for small queries or breaking entity distances. He warns that 'entity stuffing' is as bad as keyword stuffing. The biggest obstacle is training authors to think semantically. He notes that semantics is about 'how you think' and cannot be learned quickly. He advises protecting project names to prevent competitors from copying. He highlights that 'comparative ranking' means the best content today can become the worst tomorrow, requiring continuous improvement. He also points out that the human side (client skepticism, author training) often outweighs algorithmic challenges. He stresses that case studies should be long and detailed, citing multiple websites to prove a point.
